reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy defined by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury

It arises from dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, commonly through variants in regulators such as complement factor H, factor I or membrane cofactor protein (CD46), or gain-of-function variants in C3 or factor B, and sometimes anti-factor-H autoantibodies
Unlike typical HUS it is not caused by Shiga-toxin-producing organisms, and a blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with a raised lactate dehydrogenase and low haptoglobin
ADAMTS13 activity is not severely deficient, which helps separate it from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
It is often unmasked by a trigger such as infection, pregnancy, certain drugs or transplantation, on a background of genetic susceptibility
Terminal complement (C5) inhibition is the mainstay of treatment and has transformed outcomes, with plasma exchange used in some settings
There is a significant risk of recurrence, including in the renal allograft, so complement evaluation guides transplant planning
reference.pathophysiology: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is driven by uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial surfaces. Under normal conditions, regulatory proteins such as complement factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein restrain complement amplification; loss-of-function variants in these regulators, or gain-of-function variants in the C3 convertase components C3 and factor B, allow persistent complement activation and generation of the terminal membrane attack complex. The resulting endothelial injury, particularly in the renal microvasculature, promotes platelet activation and microthrombus formation, which mechanically shears red cells to produce microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, consumes platelets to cause thrombocytopenia, and obstructs glomerular capillaries to cause acute kidney injury. A genetic predisposition typically requires an environmental trigger such as infection or pregnancy to precipitate an episode.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary thrombotic microangiopathy (malignant hypertension, autoimmune disease, drugs, malignancy)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for schistocytes and thrombocytopenia
Haemolysis markers (lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, bilirubin) with a direct antiglobulin test
ADAMTS13 activity to exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Complement studies including C3, C4 and factor levels, and anti-factor-H antibodies
Stool testing for Shiga-toxin-producing organisms to exclude typical HUS
Genetic testing of complement regulator and activator genes, and renal biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Rapidly progressive acute kidney injury requiring dialysis
Neurological involvement such as seizures or altered consciousness
reference.prognosis: Before complement-targeted therapy many patients progressed to end-stage kidney disease or died; terminal complement inhibition has greatly improved renal and overall outcomes, though prognosis still depends on the underlying genetic variant and the promptness of treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal ADAMTS13 excludes a microangiopathy, or delaying treatment while awaiting genetic results
Confusing it with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and mismanaging accordingly
Attributing the picture to typical HUS and withholding complement-directed therapy
Forgetting meningococcal vaccination and prophylaxis considerations before complement inhibition
Underestimating the risk of recurrence in a kidney transplant
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
KDIGO / expert consensus guidance on atypical HUS
management: Terminal complement C5 inhibition with a monoclonal antibody (eculizumab or ravulizumab) as the disease-specific mainstay
Meningococcal vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics before and during complement blockade to cover encapsulated organisms
Plasma exchange or plasma infusion as a temporising measure pending complement inhibitor, and first-line combined with immunosuppression in the anti-factor-H antibody form
Supportive care: renal replacement therapy for acute kidney injury, red cell transfusion, and blood pressure control
Monitoring of haemolysis markers, platelet count and renal function to track treatment response and detect relapse
Genetic testing and counselling for complement regulator and activator variants, informing family screening and kidney transplant planning
Multidisciplinary nephrology, haematology and clinical genetics referral
